extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, psychology, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and critical survey of major theories explaining the origin and nature of laughter and humor (Freudian, Darwinian, conflict/mixture, Lippsian, Heckerian, etc.), assessing their claims and limits. The chapter evaluates competing explanatory criteria for what makes things laughable or produces comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in gratification / pleasurable satiation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The grimaces and contortions ... that characterize laughter appear first in the satisfied and satiated nursling ... This primal sense of pleasurable satiation may have furnished the smile, which ever remains the basic phenomenon of laughter.” (pleasure in the gratification of a tendency)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter (and smiling) can be explained as an expression of simple satisfaction or social gratification: examples include a satiated infant and meeting an old friend. Darwin and earlier writers emphasize laughter as an expression of mere joy or happiness; evidence cited includes children at play, affectionate reunions, and cases of those without imitation ability (Laura Bridgman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of psychic expenditure (Freud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud's recurring claim that pleasures of play, jest, wit, and humor may be explained as an “unexpected economy of psychic expenditure” or that an economizing tendency controls witty technics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by Freud to multiple kinds/stages of wit (children's play, jests, wit, tendency wit). The text records Freud's assertions (e.g., repetition of similarities produces pleasurable effects as unexpected economy) and also records criticisms: the author finds this economizing claim often asserted rather than demonstrated and sometimes inconsistent with Freud's other statements (e.g., about gratification vs release).

rubrics_metrics.name: Play and repetition as source of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Play ... appears in children while they are learning how to use words and connect thoughts ... it experiences pleasurable effects which originate from the repetition of similarities, the rediscovery of the familiar, sound-associations, etc.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children’s word-play and meaningless repetition produce pleasure that motivates continued play and is presented as the first step toward wit. Guidance notes that this play-pleasure is said to be independent of meaning and that Freud asserts but does not fully explain how this develops into adult wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation / economizing tendency in wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud's claim: in many witticisms “some sort of ‘condensation’ occurs, so that a given amount of verbal or conceptual effort conveys more than its usual amount of meaning. 'A compressing or — to be more exact — an economizing tendency controls all these technics.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud provides examples to show condensation, but the author objects that some examples (e.g., the 'Gold Mine / Gold Spoon / Gold Cure' joke) require more psychic effort, not less. The guidance includes a note that Freud’s evidence here is contested and that condensation may not always reduce effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency-wit: gratification vs release of inhibited energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two competing Freudian accounts: (a) pleasure in tendency-wit ‘results from the fact that a tendency whose gratification would otherwise remain unfulfilled is gratified’; (b) pleasure arises because 'the energy which had been employed in preventing its fulfilment is released' — i.e., economy of expenditure in suppressions and inhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter flags this as a central confusion in Freud: whether pleasure comes from fulfilment of impulses or from release of energy previously invested in repression. Use as a criterion requires specifying which mechanism is operative; the text criticizes Freud for failing to reconcile the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as 'economy of expenditure in feeling' (descending incongruity / Lipps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud (following Lipps/Spencer) on humor: the laughable object is often 'less impressive' than expected and the pleasure arises from an 'economy of expenditure in feeling' — the prepared feeling (sympathy, anger, compassion, etc.) proves excessive, and relief at the saving of passion causes laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to cases where expectation prepares a strong emotion that turns out to be unnecessary. The author notes this is essentially Lipps’s 'descending incongruity' reframed; Freud adopts it but does not extend it beyond that rescript. Use when judging whether an event is laughable due to reduced emotional import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the unconscious and repression in certain vivid wit forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud’s positive contribution: invention of the unconscious and the idea that repressed infantile motives surface in dreams, slips, myths, poetry and in certain 'hilarious forms of wit' — implying some witticisms require an unconsciousist account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author concedes that while Freud did not fully explain wit, his hypothesis of unconscious motives is necessary for explaining many explicit, sexual, or otherwise repressed contents appearing in jokes. Criterion: some jokes demand an account in terms of repression/unconscious content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between comic emotion and mere interpretation (dreams vs jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that release an impulse produce a comic emotion which interpreted dreams do not; Freud fails to account for this special quality of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to evaluate theories: they should explain why the same content when rendered as a joke arouses comic emotion, but when appearing in a dream (or its interpretation) does not. The chapter uses this as a key objection to Freud's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian/social / gregarious-instinct origin of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin: 'Laughter seems primarily to be the expression of mere joy or happiness' and may be understood as an act — 'a fulfilment in its own proper degree of the social instinct' whose expression is smiling and laughter in companionship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin’s observational evidence (children at play, joyful reunions, animal calls and charm) is presented as placing the origin of laughter in social/gregarious behavior rather than purely cerebral mechanisms. The text advises distrusting theories of humor that do not accord with this social/joyful foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-mixture / contrast theory of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A large tradition defines humor as a 'contrast,' 'conflict,' or 'mixture' of desirable with undesirable qualities — e.g., the sublime with the trivial, or pleasure mixed with pain — producing a double or ambivalent emotional response that yields laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rubric covers Joubert, Mendelssohn, Lessing, German romantics, Vischer, Hegel, Schopenhauer, Lipps, etc. Guidance: the contrast typically must be 'harmless' or 'of no weight' (Mendelssohn) and often involves a blending or resolution of opposites (Lessing, Vischer). The author evaluates several philosophical elaborations and their attempts to solve why the mixture increases pleasurable value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling as model / physiological analogue for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Any true science of humor must include explanation of tickling; Joubert and Hecker propose that tickling arouses a light mixture of pain and pleasure and that similar peripheral/sympathetic stimulations underlie laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as comparative evidence: physiologists (Hecker) observed peripheral nerve stimulation, pupil dilation, and invoked changes in blood-pressure and sympathetic activity to explain laughter/tickling. The chapter notes limits: tickling is peculiar and laughter follows it only in certain moods, so analogies to general comic laughter are suggestive but fragile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic 'damming' / inhibition increasing comic value (Lipps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipps’s idea: when prepared for something sublime but encountering a little thing, 'psychic damming' leaves energy ready to invest in later appreciation; humor's mission is to make the sublime appear lovable and to seek sublimity in the concealed or lowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion emphasizes that inhibition/retention of psychic energy can heighten subsequent appreciation; used to explain why contrast sometimes enhances the positive element. Critically, this is one of several attempts to explain why mixture yields amplified pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast must admit blending / not be too sharp (Lessing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing: 'The ridiculous requires a contrast between perfections and imperfections... this contrast must not be too sharp and decided, but that the opposites must be such as admit of being blended into each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical standard for what is laughable: contrasts that can be reconciled or blended are funnier than outright, irreconcilable oppositions. Use when assessing whether a juxtaposition will produce humor versus offense or disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation / intermittent alternation between pleasure and pain (Hecker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hecker’s definition: comic feeling consists of 'a rapid oscillation back and forth between pleasure and pain' of approximately equal strength, producing an intermittent, rhythmically interrupted joyful excitation (an 'intermittent joyful surprise').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hecker argues this alternation stimulates the sympathetic system in a way analogous to visual 'Glanz', emphasizing the pleasant element; the author treats this as an elegant physiological psychology but notes the analogy's frailty and the special character of tickling as a counterexample.
